strategy.headline: Utah buys Jazz gear five kids at a time, dressed for the canyon and measured against Stockton and Malone.
strategy.thesis: Jazz fans drive in from Ogden, Logan, Provo, St. George, southern Idaho and Wyoming, and they buy as families, kids first. Taste comes from a thin layer: the all-ages DIY scene in Sugar House and the Granary District, and West Side Pacific Islander and Latino families. Those families rank church-ward, rec and high school basketball with football. The Stockton-Malone-Sloan era is the moral standard, a younger crowd grew up on the Mitchell-Gobert playoff years, and everyone wears technical outdoor layers as everyday clothes. The City Edition is a gray-gradient repeat and there's no opening-night, Christmas or Specter stage, so the Oct 30 home Cup night against Denver is the one fixed date. Land a Peterson-and-Bailey family program before the Oct 20 tip-off, then sell it as a local family gift through the Cup nights to Three Kings Day. After that, turn the gray gradient into Utah material in Nike's own cold-weather layers, and pitch Salt Line now as the 2027-28 City Edition.

archetype.name: The Statewide Family Loyalist
archetype.description: A fan who drives in on I-15 with three kids in purple youth jerseys and measures every new star against Stockton and Malone. The January walk to the Delta Center is cold, so it's a puffer and a beanie. Loyal to the team over any brand, patient with a rebuild, allergic to hype.

pulse.teamMoment: Coming off 22-60, Utah is speeding up its youth movement. No. 2 pick Darryn Peterson and Ace Bailey join Lauri Markkanen and Jaren Jackson Jr. Walker Kessler went to the Lakers for future firsts, and Jaxson Hayes and Josh Okogie came in. Will Hardy is under pressure to develop them, and BetMGM's 35.5-win total asks for about 13 more wins.
pulse.sentiment: Impatient but curious. Fans are tired after a bottom-of-the-league year and energized by Peterson and the Jackson Jr. trade. They expect visible progress and a play-in chase, not a playoff run.

topInsights.title: The repeat City Edition needs new material
topInsights.insight: The vertical gray gradient with baby blue trim is back for a second straight season, so there's no debut spike to sell. Every lens maps that gray onto something locals live with: winter inversion haze, Wasatch granite, the salt crust of the Bonneville flats, a clear high-desert sky after a storm.
topInsights.implication: Texture is the refresh: salt-crackle print, granite-speckle fleece, inversion-to-sky fades. Never market it as new, and save the big story for the next City Edition.

topInsights.title: Buy for five kids, not one collector
topInsights.insight: Utah has the largest average household and the youngest median age of any state. Families buy Jazz gear in multiples, on a once-a-season trip to the Delta Center, a Murray or Orem mall, or Dick's. Deseret Industries thrifting and value-tier buying are normal. Authentic jerseys are a small collector niche.
topInsights.implication: Lead with deep youth and toddler sizing in the current Mountain Purple, black and sky blue palette. Add matching kid-to-adult sets and bundle-friendly entry tees. Keep premium to a small tier, clearly set apart.

topInsights.title: Canyon wardrobe is game-night wardrobe
topInsights.insight: Locals ski Alta, Snowbird and Brighton after work and hoop in cold church and rec-center gyms all winter. Technical shells, fleece and snap-pocket layers are everyday clothes. From November through March, fans head to the Delta Center in puffers, fleece and beanies.
topInsights.implication: Outerwear and layering belong at the core of the Jazz assortment, inside Nike's own ACG and NBA outerwear lanes. Borrow local technical codes (shell cuts, snap pockets, drawcords) instead of partnering with outdoor competitors.

topInsights.title: Three eras and an untold origin
topInsights.insight: Fans split into Note-era (1979-96) and 1996 Mountain-era loyalists, and younger fans thrift both at DI and cut them up. Fans now in their 20s grew up on the 2017-22 Donovan Mitchell and Rudy Gobert playoff teams. Everyone knows the 'no jazz in Utah' joke and the New Orleans start, but no product tells it well.
topInsights.implication: Run separate era capsules instead of mixing palettes, with a Mitchell-Gobert chapter that bridges to Peterson. Put the New Orleans origin on labels and inserts with the team mark, not a player name. First, confirm which licensee holds heritage jerseys.

topInsights.title: The West Side: big on hoops, barely served
topInsights.insight: Rose Park, Glendale, West Valley and Kearns hold one of the highest per-capita Pacific Islander populations in the US, plus large Latino communities. They're a major part of the valley's youth basketball and football, from church-ward leagues to high school programs. Yet they have few premium doors and appear on almost no Jazz product.
topInsights.implication: Co-create a capsule with paid, credited Tongan, Samoan and Latino designers, each community with its own credit and approval rights. Use PIK2AR and Centro Civico Mexicano for cultural review and access, not as design studios. Never lift tatau, tapa or ceremonial patterns.

topInsights.title: Utah taste grew up all-ages
topInsights.insight: Utah is young and has few under-21 rooms, so its scene grew up in all-ages venues like Kilby Court. SLUG Magazine documented it, and SLUG's screen-printed flyers and Gallery Stroll openings are the local graphic language.
topInsights.implication: The lifestyle graphic language is gig-poster screen prints, hand-lettered date blocks and cassette and 7-inch packaging, in Jazz purple, black and sky blue inks. Keep bar imagery and jokes about the state's religious culture off the line.

topInsights.title: One fixed stage, then local quiet zones
topInsights.insight: The Jazz aren't on the opening-night or Christmas slate, so the confirmed Oct 30 home Cup night against Denver is the season's only fixed in-arena stage. General Conference empties the first weekends of April and October. Many households keep Sunday as a family day, and Halloween is a major neighborhood night. In summer, July 24 Pioneer Day outranks any NBA date.
topInsights.implication: Tie the launch to dates already certain: product in doors by Sat Oct 17, the Oct 30 Cup night, Black Friday. Stage in-person drops on Fridays and Saturdays, and avoid Oct 31. Push Sunday demand to digital, and run December to Jan 6 as local family gifting.

uniform.narrative: The state's namesake lake is shrinking, and its salt crust, shoreline contours and Bonneville land-speed culture are shared Utah icons. A dark shale City Edition with tonal shoreline contours, salt-white numerals and land-speed lettering tells a story only Utah can wear. It stays clear of the white Association uniform and anchors in Mountain Purple. Pitch it now for 2027-28, the first open slot after two seasons of the gray gradient. This season's salt-crackle outerwear and January poster tee are the fan tests. If 2027-28 is already locked, it ships as an August 2027 lifestyle capsule and the uniform moves to 2028-29.

scorecard.rationale: Whole-state, family-sized loyalty keeps fandom near the league average, but a small metro in a rebuild with no national stage and a thin boutique layer sits near the bottom on opportunity, culture and retail (brief scores: opportunity 52, culture 66, retail 40, fandom 68). A small metro, but the buyer base is the whole state: family-sized, youth-heavy and loyal to one team. Its design vocabulary is unusually distinct (salt, snow, all-ages DIY, West Side hoops). Retail is spread along I-15 with a thin boutique layer, and a rebuild year with no national stage caps the near-term upside.

music.headline: Salt Lake sings in four-part harmony and screams in all-ages basements.
music.summary: Salt Lake music runs on two engines. One is institutional: the Tabernacle Choir, the Utah Symphony and clean-cut pop from the Osmonds to Neon Trees. The other is a stubborn DIY underground of all-ages rooms like Kilby Court, KRCL community radio and SLUG Magazine. That scene's flyer and poster language can give the gray City Edition a voice.

insights.title: The name is the story nobody tells
insights.detail: The Jazz were named in New Orleans and moved to Utah in 1979, so the franchise carries a genre name with no local jazz roots. Utah has a real if small jazz scene. The link is mostly typographic and nostalgic, not sonic. The name sits in a market that rarely sings about it.
insights.implication: Pair a local jazz-and-improv voice with product, so the name is earned rather than ironic. A New Orleans-to-Wasatch story could anchor a capsule.

insights.title: Credibility is earned in all-ages rooms
insights.detail: Utah's alcohol laws and young population made all-ages rooms like Kilby Court in the Granary District the proving ground for generations of bands. Gig posters, screen-printed flyers and SLUG Magazine culture set the visual language.
insights.implication: Screen-print and flyer looks read as real here, and a polished stadium-rock look would not. Use them for tees and hoodies.

insights.title: Choir culture shapes how the city hears harmony
insights.detail: The Tabernacle Choir, the Utah Symphony at Abravanel Hall, and ward and stake music mean many locals grew up singing in parts. The anthem and group singalongs land with unusual unity in an arena.
insights.implication: Leave sacred and church imagery alone. Build on celebratory, communal sound instead, such as crowd-sung moments and sound-wave graphics.

insights.title: Hometown exports give the market swagger
insights.detail: Imagine Dragons formed in Provo and Las Vegas with BYU roots. Neon Trees came out of Provo, and the Osmonds out of Ogden defined an earlier era. A Provo-to-Orem emo and pop-punk lineage runs beside them. Utah claims these acts as its own even when they live elsewhere.
insights.implication: Artist collaborations need licensing and likely run through management. The safer route is crediting local-scene lineage in editorial content, with no logos or lyrics.

insights.title: The West Side holds the rhythm
insights.detail: Rose Park and Glendale are home to Mexican-American and Pacific Islander communities, with their own church choirs, quinceanera and family-party music, and lowrider and cumbia culture. You hear it at community gatherings far more than at downtown venues.
insights.implication: Work through community partners and pay local creators. Never lift Polynesian motifs without a collaborator.

insights.title: A young roster meets a young audience
insights.detail: Darryn Peterson and Ace Bailey play beside Lauri Markkanen and Jaren Jackson Jr. The team's story is youth and development, which mirrors Utah's youngest-in-the-nation demographic and its music-making teenagers.
insights.implication: Build drops around emerging local artists, not legacy acts, to rhyme with the rebuild.

art.headline: Salt Lake looks like salt, snow and sandstone, drawn on a grid and printed by hand.
art.summary: Salt Lake's visual culture sits between an orderly city grid and an outdoor-art tradition. The working scene is artist-run and DIY, from Central 9th, Sugar House and downtown to Craft Lake City and the Utah Arts Festival. Dress the gray City Edition in real Utah materials and local makers, not mountain clip art. Keep LDS sacred imagery off it, and never flatten Pacific Islander culture into decoration.

insights.title: The grid is the graphic language
insights.detail: Salt Lake addresses are coordinates: 900 South and 900 East, shortened locally to 9th and 9th, or 2100 South, or "the West Side." Residents use these numbers as neighborhood identity. They sit beside the beehive iconography and mid-century signage that give the city its orderly look.
insights.implication: Put numeric grid coordinates in a clean sans on tees, jock tags and hangtags. They are more ownable than another mountain silhouette, and nobody else can swap them in.

insights.title: Salt, snow and shale beat generic mountain
insights.detail: The current Jazz City Edition is a vertical gray gradient with baby blue trim. It maps onto Wasatch granite, inversion haze and winter dawn, and onto the pale texture of the Bonneville Salt Flats and the Great Salt Lake shoreline.
insights.implication: Build graphics from real surfaces: crusted salt, shale, snow-pack. Then the gray palette reads as place, not a default colorway.

insights.title: Land art is the city's signature art world
insights.detail: Utah is a land-art pilgrimage. Robert Smithson built Spiral Jetty at Rozel Point on the Great Salt Lake in 1970, and Nancy Holt set her Sun Tunnels in the Great Basin desert in 1976. The lake's low water and pink microbial color shifts are a live civic concern.
insights.implication: A spiral or shoreline-contour motif can anchor a collection. Credit and license anything derived from Smithson's work (estate and Holt-Smithson Foundation), and consider a Great Salt Lake conservation tie-in.

insights.title: Artist-run DIY and print culture drives the scene
insights.detail: Monthly Gallery Stroll, Craft Lake City's DIY Fest, screen-print and poster shops, and the downtown and Central 9th studio clusters feed the scene. It runs on local illustrators and muralists more than on a gallery market.
insights.implication: Commission two or three local artists through a paid, credited program for a limited graphic drop. Don't source a single "Utah" look in Portland.

insights.title: Two Jazz eras, both worth drawing
insights.detail: The franchise carries the 1979-96 musical-note look and the 1996-2004 purple, teal and copper mountain era. Its New Orleans legacy is heritage to Utah fans, not baggage.
insights.implication: Run purple-and-mountain throwbacks beside the gray City Edition as a heritage lane. Check licensing on legacy marks with the team and NBA.

insights.title: West Side culture is visually underserved
insights.detail: Utah has one of the largest per-capita Pacific Islander populations in the US, concentrated in West Valley City, Kearns, Rose Park and Glendale. Glendale and Rose Park also have a visible Latino presence. Community anchors include Centro Civico Mexicano and the Mestizo Institute of Culture and Arts, both to be confirmed as active. The Jazz come off a 22-60 season, but a young core of Darryn Peterson, Ace Bailey, Lauri Markkanen and Jaren Jackson Jr. brings fresh fans from these communities.
insights.implication: Co-create with community designers, tattoo artists and church or school groups. Never lift tatau, tapa or other ceremonial patterns without family or community permission and payment.

food.headline: Salt Lake runs on dirty soda and fry sauce. The West Side cooks the rest.
food.summary: Utah food is homegrown and a little peculiar: fry sauce, funeral potatoes, Jell-O (the state snack), honey-butter scones and the dirty-soda cup. Utah-born chains carry more daily pride than any fine-dining name. Underneath, Mexican and Pacific Islander kitchens on the West Side and along the I-15 corridor feed the city. The way in is snack-shop humor and drink-cup color, not one restaurant's logo.

insights.title: The dirty-soda cup is the local status object
insights.detail: Swig (founded in St. George in 2010) and rivals like Sodalicious and Fiiz made cream-and-syrup fountain soda in a branded foam or tumbler cup a daily Utah ritual. Many residents skip coffee and alcohol, and the large LDS population's abstention is part of the reason. The cups show up at every game, school and office.
insights.implication: A cup-shaped graphic, ice-pellet texture or soda-fountain colorway reads as Utah at once and steers clear of alcohol branding. Pair it with the City Edition's baby-blue trim.

insights.title: Crown Burgers and the Greek-built pastrami burger
insights.detail: The Salt Lake pastrami burger, piled with fry sauce, comes from the valley's Greek immigrant restaurant tradition. Crown Burgers carries it, and it is a locals-only order. Fry sauce is the shared state condiment, closely tied to Arctic Circle.
insights.implication: Fry-sauce pink and pastrami-burger wrapper graphics are insider shorthand. Anything using a brand name needs a licensing or collaboration conversation first.

insights.title: Utah-born fast casual is civic pride
insights.detail: Cafe Rio and Costa Vida (sweet pork barbacoa, tortilla-pressed salads) started in Utah, and locals brag about them. Arctic Circle, Hires Big H and Crown are older drive-in names that get the same treatment.
insights.implication: A collaboration or nod-and-wink product with a hometown chain beats a generic local-food reference. All use needs licensed marks, so start outreach early.

insights.title: West Side Mexican food is the real flavor
insights.detail: Red Iguana on North Temple (family-run since 1985, known for its seven moles) draws pilgrims, locals and visitors alike. Panaderias and taquerias line Redwood Road and State Street, and the Rose Park and Glendale corridors hold more of both, with quinceanera culture. The Latino community is among the Jazz's most loyal and least marketed-to fan bases.
insights.implication: Work with West Side makers on artwork and language. Don't borrow chile or mole iconography. Credit and pay them.

insights.title: Pacific Islander feast culture reaches the stands
insights.detail: Utah has one of the largest per-capita Polynesian populations in the US, with strong Tongan and Samoan families and church networks. Community catering and church feasts (lu, palusami, oka, pua'a roasts) and big-family gatherings are central. Local hoops, football and rugby talent comes out of these communities.
insights.implication: Go through community partners and Polynesian designers for any pattern work. Never lift tapa, tatau or ceremonial imagery.

insights.title: Game day is beer-light and dessert-heavy
insights.detail: Pre-game runs through the Squatters and Wasatch brewpubs and Beer Bar (co-owned by actor Ty Burrell) near downtown. The larger family crowd leans on soda shops, scones, ice cream and Jell-O-style nostalgia. Utah's alcohol rules and LDS norms shape every food decision.
insights.implication: Lead with soda, honey, scones and dessert for broad-reach product. Keep alcohol references to a quiet niche capsule.

culture.headline: Utah feels underestimated by the coasts, and the Jazz turn that chip into noise.
culture.summary: Salt Lake City is a mountain-and-desert hometown with pioneer roots, fast-growing communities and a work-hard, low-ego streak. It assumes the rest of the country boils it down to one religion and one stereotype. Pride runs through terrain, the beehive and the Jazz, who have carried the state's name since 1979. Design from the land and its heritage, not nightlife or street cliches.

insights.title: The small-market chip, worn lightly
insights.detail: Utahns joke that national media overlook and misread them. They answer with quiet pride and a loud arena, not swagger. The Jazz have always been the underdog that outworks bigger markets.
insights.implication: Keep the tone earned and understated. Lead with craft, material and place-specific detail, not hype slogans or flash.

insights.title: The mountain is the skyline
insights.detail: The Wasatch wall behind downtown is the shared symbol, and many locals ski Alta, Snowbird, Brighton or Solitude on a weekday after work. The Jazz's Mountain-era branding and the current gray-gradient City Edition both speak that language.
insights.implication: Gradients, ridgelines and snow-and-slate palettes read as local without a city name. They also layer well into outerwear-influenced product.

insights.title: Beehive and Deseret: everyday civic marks
insights.detail: The beehive is on the state flag, road signs, buildings and beer taps. It stands for industry and cooperation, and it belongs to no single institution. Pioneer Day on July 24 is a state holiday with its own parades, fireworks and family rituals.
insights.implication: A clean beehive or honeycomb geometry is a safe, instantly recognized motif. Keep it civic, and stay away from church-owned imagery and temple iconography.

insights.title: The West Side is the city's fastest-changing core
insights.detail: Rose Park, Glendale, Kearns and West Valley City hold large Polynesian (Tongan, Samoan), Latino and refugee communities. Utah has one of the highest per-capita Pacific Islander populations in the country. Football and basketball courts and church gyms anchor the neighborhoods.
insights.implication: Partner with community artists and organizations, and pay them. Never borrow tatau, tapa or other ceremonial patterning as decoration.

insights.title: Two valleys, two rivalries, one state
insights.detail: Family loyalties split three ways: the University of Utah Utes in red, the BYU Cougars in Provo in blue and the Utah State Aggies in Logan in navy. The Utes-BYU game is called the Holy War. The Jazz are one of the few things that pull all three camps into one arena.
insights.implication: Skip college-adjacent colorways that look like they favor a school. Stick to neutral state-level cues and Jazz-owned palettes.

insights.title: Outdoor life defines the wardrobe
insights.detail: Fleece, puffer jackets, trail shoes and cap-and-hoodie combinations pass as downtown dress, and a winter night at Delta Center means layers. Summers are dry and hot, with strong UV and dust in the high desert. Church, family and game-night dress codes skew modest.
insights.implication: Prioritize warm-up jackets, vests, quarter-zips, heavyweight fleece and weather-ready fabrics. The product should work before and after a night out in the cold.

insights.title: The Great Salt Lake is both pride and anxiety
insights.detail: The shrinking shoreline and the dust are a live civic topic. The salt flats, the pink north arm and Spiral Jetty are shared visual icons. Locals care about water and air quality.
insights.implication: Salt-white and lake-pink accents are distinctive. Handle any lake-themed product with care, and ideally tie it to a conservation partner rather than using the lake as pure decoration.

underground.headline: Along the Wasatch Front, snow, skate and DIY music share one scene.
underground.summary: Taste here is set between mountain and city. Skate and snowboard crews overlap, all-ages rooms like Kilby Court carry DIY music, and Rose Park and Glendale bring lowrider, Polynesian and Latino style. Queer nightlife and Pride are bigger and better organized than outsiders assume. Come in through shops, crews and community orgs, not the Delta Center, and pay the creators you credit.

insights.title: Snow and skate are one scene
insights.detail: Wasatch snowboard and skate crews overlap. Alta, Brighton and Park City resort culture sits a canyon away from the skate spots in Sugar House and Ogden. The uniform is Carhartt workwear, beanies, technical shells and skate shoes, not fashion-forward streetwear.
insights.implication: Weather-ready basketball product (shell textures, utility pockets, fleece) fits better than hype-driven drops. Pair Jazz warm-up and shell jackets with the Ogden outdoor-industry crowd.

insights.title: 90s Jazz gear is what thrifters hunt
insights.detail: Locals thrift, restore and cut up the purple Mountain and Note-era Stockton-and-Malone gear. It signals older-sibling and parent loyalty to the Jazz, and it's a nostalgia code shared across Mormon-majority suburbs and the West Side alike. The 2026-27 young core and the gray City Edition give a newer way in.
insights.implication: Reissue-style graphics and a purple-copper Mountain palette will land on heritage product, but only with a licensed, accurate Jazz vintage identity. Pushing the 2026-27 youth movement (Peterson, Bailey) can bridge old and new.

insights.title: The West Side drives culture, uncredited
insights.detail: Rose Park and Glendale hold a Polynesian (Tongan, Samoan) and Latino community. It shapes football-first, family-and-church street style, lowrider and truck culture, and cruising rituals. Utah's Pacific Islander population is among the highest per capita in the US.
insights.implication: Work through community orgs and local designers, and pay them. Collaborate on tapa and tatau-inspired pattern only with explicit approval from its cultural owners. Never lift sacred motifs.

insights.title: DIY music rooms set the weekend
insights.detail: All-ages and DIY venues anchor the punk, emo and hardcore crowds. Think Kilby Court (Granary/Rio Grande area) and the Urban Lounge on Fifth East, plus record stores like Diabolical and Randy's. Merch culture means band tees, thrifted sport jerseys and screenprints.
insights.implication: Make a small run of screenprinted warm-up tees and practice jerseys, and sell or gift them through DIY rooms. That reaches taste-setters better than a flagship launch.

insights.title: Queer nightlife is organized and visible
insights.detail: Utah Pride (June) and a long-running bar and drag circuit give SLC an openly queer culture that contradicts its image. Ballroom and drag crowds remix athletic wear with glam.
insights.implication: Work on Pride-season product only through local queer organizations and artists, with real partnership and payment. A seasonal logo swap won't do.

insights.title: Salt flats and speed culture
insights.detail: The Bonneville Salt Flats and Speed Week at Wendover feed a hot-rod, land-speed and custom-car culture unlike coastal lowrider scenes. Its look is white salt, chrome, hand-painted numerals and pinstriping.
insights.implication: Pinstripes and racing-number typography are a Utah-only graphic idea for City Edition-adjacent product, and they fit the gray-gradient palette.

hoops.headline: In Utah, winter basketball happens in church gyms.
hoops.summary: Basketball in the Salt Lake valley lives as much indoors as out. Winter pushes the game into LDS ward meetinghouse gyms, rec centers and high school fieldhouses, and summer brings park courts and the Salt Lake City Summer League. After 22-60, the Jazz are betting on Peterson, Bailey, Markkanen and Jaren Jackson Jr., and fans are hopeful but wary.

insights.title: The gym is the court
insights.detail: Long, snowy winters and a dense network of church meetinghouse gyms and city rec centers push most local hooping indoors. Leagues come with scorekeepers and church-ball rules. Outdoor park courts peak from May through September.
insights.implication: Build product around gym-to-street versatility: a shoe and apparel kit that goes from hardwood rec leagues to a snowy walk in. Summer-court graphics alone won't do.

insights.title: Utah vs. BYU is the college fault line
insights.detail: The Utes and the BYU Cougars share a long rivalry with religious, cultural and geographic weight, now played with both schools in the Big 12 after realignment. Utah State and Weber State hold their own northern-Utah loyalties. College loyalty splits along all four lines, and Utah-BYU is the emotional center.
insights.implication: Keep college colors out of Jazz product, and keep the Jazz and campus lanes separate. Consider licensed collegiate collaborations only with each school as its own partner.

insights.title: Old heroes for parents, rookies for now
insights.detail: The Stockton-and-Malone era and the Mailman identity still anchor adult fandom. This season's hope rests on Peterson, Bailey, Markkanen and Jackson. Fans are optimistic, but the team went 22-60 last year.
insights.implication: Pair heritage cues with youth-forward product. Offer retro purple-mountain energy for parents, and the current gray City Edition and player-led drops for the next generation.

insights.title: West Side families fill the gyms
insights.detail: Rose Park, Glendale and the broader West Side valley communities, including large Tongan, Samoan and Latino populations, bring family-centered rec ball, tournaments, and church and community leagues. They sit apart from the Jazz's mainstream image. The West Side supplies much of the hoops energy the valley's postcard image leaves out.
insights.implication: Work through community organizations and local coaches, not imagery. Commission Pacific Islander and Latino designers and credit them. Never lift sacred tatau or ceremonial patterns.

insights.title: No WNBA team, but a Starzz memory
insights.detail: Utah had the WNBA's Starzz from 1997 to 2002, before the franchise moved to San Antonio, so older fans remember women's pro ball here. The Jazz's G League affiliate, the Salt Lake City Stars, is the local pro product.
insights.implication: Women's hooper programming and Stars-level events are open space. A Starzz-inspired heritage capsule is a possible story, subject to licensing.

insights.title: Outdoor-life crossover is the local style
insights.detail: Valley hoopers dress like Wasatch locals: technical shells, trail-run and ski-adjacent layers, and mountain-town athleisure over hoop gear. BYU and Utah school colors show at games.
insights.implication: Build cold-weather hoop layers, shooting shells and warm-up pieces with mountain-range and snow-gradient graphics that echo the Jazz gray City Edition.

fanbase.headline: From Logan to St. George, the Jazz are the whole state's team.
fanbase.summary: The Jazz are the only major men's team that belongs to all of Utah, from Sugar House and the West Side to the small towns along I-15 and I-80. Fans prize the 1990s Finals teams, blue-collar discipline and small-market pride. After 22-60 they're impatient but curious. Loyalty runs to the team and its eras first, ahead of any Nike swoosh.

insights.title: The 1990s set the standard
insights.detail: Stockton, Malone and Jerry Sloan reached back-to-back Finals in 1997 and 1998. They define a Jazz team: pick-and-roll, toughness, no flash. Fans hold every new star to that standard and distrust hype.
insights.implication: Lead with heritage product: the Jazz Note, the purple mountain, Stockton-Malone silhouettes through licensing. Don't go futurist. The youth movement needs a bridge to the past.

insights.title: Statewide, not citywide
insights.detail: With no other major men's franchise in the state, a Jazz hoodie is as common in Logan, St. George, Ogden and Provo as in Salt Lake. Many fans drive in on I-15 for a handful of games a year and treat the Delta Center as a day trip.
insights.implication: Plan drops and pop-ups along the Wasatch Front and in northern and southern Utah. Build outerwear and travel-friendly layers, not just city streetwear.

insights.title: Rebuild patience is thin but real
insights.detail: The team went 22-60 last season. Then the Peterson pick and the future firsts from the Kessler sign-and-trade turned talk toward the long game. The win total sits around 35.5, so fans expect visible progress, not a playoff push.
insights.implication: Time rookie and young-player product for the first home stretch and the Oct 30 NBA Cup night versus Denver. Sell hope and development, not a title.

insights.title: Color loyalty is split across eras
insights.detail: Purple and teal with the copper mountain stir 1990s nostalgia. The highlighter-yellow looks of the early 2020s were short-lived and are history. The newest layer is the current Mountain Purple, Midnight Black and Sky Blue identity, plus the gray-gradient City Edition with baby blue trim. Fans argue over eras the way they argue over coaching.
insights.implication: Offer separate era capsules so nostalgic and current fans each see their own team. Don't mix palettes in one piece.

insights.title: Faith, family and the outdoors shape gameday
insights.detail: Utah's family-heavy culture and strong Latter-day Saint presence make many games family outings, with early-evening routines and alcohol-light gamedays. The outdoor lifestyle (ski, hike, climb) shows up in what fans wear.
insights.implication: Design for kids and families, with modest cuts and technical outerwear. Keep the tone warm and wholesome, and never caricature the state's religion.

insights.title: A second arena tenant raises the stakes
insights.detail: The Delta Center name returned in 2023, and the arena now also hosts the NHL's Utah team. Downtown nights compete for the same fans and merch dollars. Jazz loyalists defend their tenure as the older claim.
insights.implication: Give Jazz product an "original" tone: heritage marks, founding-year details and the New Orleans-to-Utah story. Avoid anything that reads as generic Utah sports.

rhythm.headline: The Jazz year peaks twice: a hopeful fall, then June's draft and July's Summer League
rhythm.summary: Coming off 22-60, the Jazz sell hope and development in 2026-27, not playoff gear. Attention peaks at the October opener and Cup night, then the holiday gift window, and spring rides on the play-in hunt. Ski season, Utes and BYU football, the Mammoth, Real Salt Lake and General Conference all compete. Draft night and Summer League are real events here, because this fan base buys into prospects.

insights.title: Opening weeks are the biggest buying window
insights.detail: The season tips off Oct 20. The Jazz host Denver on opening Cup night, Oct 30, in West Group A with DEN, HOU, PHX and DAL. Fans are fresh off a draft that landed the No. 2 pick, Darryn Peterson, and Ace Bailey is in year two.
insights.implication: Launch Peterson and Bailey player product and the new-season Association and Icon drops by mid-October, so fans have them in hand for Cup night.

insights.title: A repeat City Edition means no debut
insights.detail: The vertical gray gradient with baby blue trim was announced for both 2025-26 and 2026-27. There is no new debut to spike the winter.
insights.implication: Skip the debut event. Refresh the gray-gradient capsule instead, with new graphics, outerwear and warm-ups, and tie it to the new rookies.

insights.title: Winter belongs to ski season and the holidays
insights.detail: Alta, Snowbird, Brighton and Solitude open around late November. December gift-giving is heavily family-centered. The Jazz are not on the Christmas Day or opening-night slates, so the holidays are local, not national.
insights.implication: Design a Jazz cold-weather line (puffer vests, fleece, beanies) that works on the mountain and in the Delta Center. Market it as gifts in November and December.

insights.title: Spring depends on the standings
insights.detail: BetMGM sets the win total at 35.5, about 13 better than last year. The realistic target is the play-in, Apr 13-16, after the regular season ends Apr 11. LDS General Conference takes the first weekend of April.
insights.implication: Hold back playoff-style gear and keep spring to player-led and lifestyle items. Push a play-in capsule only if Utah is in the 7-10 range by mid-March.

insights.title: The offseason has real events
insights.detail: The draft in late June and Salt Lake City Summer League at the Delta Center in July pull fans in even when the team is quiet. The roster is built on prospects.
insights.implication: Make a draft-night rookie reveal and a Summer League pop-up the summer anchors. Don't plan on a quiet June through August.

insights.title: One arena, many Utah teams
insights.detail: The Delta Center also hosts the NHL's Utah Mammoth. The Utes, BYU and Real Salt Lake share the calendar, so fans split their attention in fall and summer.
insights.implication: Avoid purple-only product that reads as generic Utah pride. Keep Jazz marks (the note, the gradient) distinct from the Mammoth and the colleges.

uniform.headline: The Jazz wear a New Orleans name against the Wasatch, and the best uniforms tell both
uniform.summary: The franchise moved from New Orleans in 1979 and kept the Jazz name, the purple-gold-green palette and the music note. Fans love the Note and Mountain eras most, and today's Mountain Purple, Midnight Black and Sky Blue look is still earning its place. With the City Edition on repeat, the open ground is Utah's non-LDS story: the West Side, the Great Salt Lake, the salt flats and the 2002 Olympics.

insights.title: The palette is a Mardi Gras inheritance
insights.detail: New Orleans chose purple, gold and green in 1974, and the team carried them to Salt Lake City in 1979. Many casual Utah fans no longer connect those colors to the move. Almost no uniform has told the New Orleans-to-Utah story on purpose.
insights.implication: A heritage-led Classic or City concept that credits New Orleans gives Nike a story no other Western Conference team can claim. It needs a real New Orleans partner, or it will feel like costume.

insights.title: The Note and the Mountain carry the nostalgia
insights.detail: Utah fans wear the Stockton, Malone and Jerry Sloan years under the purple note to games. They wear the 1996 mountain-skyline era, with its purple and turquoise palette, just as often. These are the two throwbacks they ask for.
insights.implication: Lead Classic Edition and lifestyle throwbacks with these two eras. Treat the 2004-2016 navy era as the secondary heritage line.

insights.title: This season's City story is a rerun
insights.detail: The vertical gray gradient with baby blue trim was announced for both 2025-26 and 2026-27. The roster turns over, but the City concept doesn't. Gray is a cool, tonal choice that sits apart from the franchise's saturated color heritage.
insights.implication: Use the repeat year to push Association, Icon and Statement, Specter-adjacent lifestyle drops and player-led product. Prepare a stronger 2027-28 City concept.

insights.title: In a rebuild, the player is the product
insights.detail: The No. 2 pick Darryn Peterson and Ace Bailey arrive alongside Lauri Markkanen and Jaren Jackson Jr. after a 22-60 season. The win total sits near 35.5. A young lineup invites new-fan and family-size demand.
insights.implication: Plan Peterson and Bailey jersey and tee runs, youth sizing and signature-adjacent graphics early. Give Markkanen's Finnish following its own Finland-facing capsule.

insights.title: Outdoor Utah is the strongest visual language
insights.detail: Wasatch ski and trail culture, the Great Salt Lake shoreline, red-rock southern Utah and the Bonneville salt flats each have colors and textures locals recognize. Local outdoor makers such as Black Diamond, Kuhl and Voile are headquartered in or around Salt Lake.
insights.implication: Technical outerwear, warm-ups and ACG-adjacent cross-category product fit this market better than city-street imagery. They also set Utah apart from East Coast and LA-driven collections.

insights.title: West Side communities rarely appear on product
insights.detail: Salt Lake County has among the largest Pacific Islander populations per capita on the US mainland, concentrated in West Valley and the West Side. Rose Park, Glendale and Ogden have large Latino communities. Both show up at youth and high school basketball and football.
insights.implication: Co-create community capsules with credited local artists and designers, not borrowed patterns. Never use sacred tatau or ceremonial imagery.

retail-landscape.headline: The gear sells in suburban malls. The taste comes from a few downtown doors.
retail-landscape.summary: Jazz shoppers split into separate orbits along I-15: Salt Lake County, Utah County and Davis/Weber. Families buy most of the gear, and young kids steer demand. A thin downtown and Sugar House scene sets taste, while Pacific Islander and Latino families love their hoops and go underserved. With a rookie-led roster, kids' sizing is where the near-term volume is.

insights.title: The Wasatch Front shops in separate orbits
insights.detail: Downtown SLC has the Delta Center and City Creek. The south valley has Fashion Place in Murray, Jordan Landing and Sandy. Utah County (Provo/Orem/Lehi) has University Place in Orem, Provo Towne Centre and the Lehi outlets. Each has its own anchor doors and shoppers, and Davis and Weber counties (Layton/Ogden) pull from the north as a fourth.
insights.implication: Plan a corridor along I-15, not one flagship moment. Time pop-ups to game days downtown, and keep a steady wholesale presence in the suburban malls.

insights.title: Families and kids buy most of the gear
insights.detail: Utah has a very young population and big households. Much of Jazz buying is kids' and youth jerseys, tees and caps, picked up on family trips to the arena, the malls (Fanatics/Lids-style kiosks), Dick's or online.
insights.implication: Put youth and toddler sizing first. Keep Icon/Statement/City Edition tees affordable, and favor Peterson and Bailey youth jerseys over premium adult drops.

insights.title: A few doors set the taste
insights.detail: Next to LA, NYC or Portland, SLC has few full-time independent sneaker boutiques. Taste comes from Sugar House and downtown shops, vintage and Deseret Industries thrifting, skate shops and online communities.
insights.implication: A few seeded pairs, local creators and pop-ups will register here more than a broad wholesale push. Partner locally, and don't assume a boutique network exists.

insights.title: Outdoor brands carry local credibility
insights.detail: Utah is home to Black Diamond, Kuhl and Skullcandy, and to a deep ski, trail and climbing culture around the Wasatch. Shoppers move easily between hoops, trail and snow.
insights.implication: Trail- and snow-inspired textures and colors feel native, as do co-branded outdoor-hoops collaborations. Look at ACG-adjacent basketball crossovers.

insights.title: Loyal communities, few premium doors
insights.detail: Rose Park and Glendale on the West Side, plus West Valley and Utah County, have large Pacific Islander (Tongan, Samoan) and Latino communities. High school hoops and football run deep there, but premium sneaker doors are few.
insights.implication: Work through community events, schools and local creators, and pay and credit them. Get product into Foot Locker and other athletic-chain doors in those areas, not only downtown.

insights.title: The Jazz brand sits at a tipping point
insights.detail: The Jazz went 22-60 last season, then rebuilt around Peterson, Bailey, Markkanen and Jackson Jr. The win total is set at 35.5. Fan energy runs on hope, and gear demand follows the rookies.
insights.implication: Stock deeper on Peterson and Bailey than on legacy names. Tie drops to Cup nights and the Oct 30 home opener against Denver.

retail-behavior.headline: Utah shops on a family calendar: Pioneer Day, conference weekends and snow
retail-behavior.summary: The Wasatch Front is young, employed and family-sized, so spending runs to multi-unit buys, kids' sizes and gifts rather than single premium pieces. School starts, Pioneer Day, General Conference, Christmas and ski season set the calendar. With the 2026-27 Jazz rebuilding around youth, enthusiasm likely follows Markkanen, Jackson Jr., Peterson and Bailey, not playoff hopes.

insights.title: Household size drives basket size
insights.detail: Utah has the largest average household and the youngest median age of any state. Across Salt Lake, Davis, Utah and Weber counties, many families have four or more children. They tend to buy several kids' and youth pieces at once, which favors accessible prices and deep sizing.
insights.implication: Lead with a strong youth and kids' range, multi-pack or bundle-friendly tees and hoodies, and a visible entry price tier. Premium-only assortments will under-index.

insights.title: Pioneer Day and conference weekends are local peaks
insights.detail: July 24 (Pioneer Day) is a state holiday with the Days of '47 events, parades and rodeo. LDS General Conference takes over the first weekend of April and October and keeps many households home. Neither is an NBA moment, but both decide when families are free to shop and gather.
insights.implication: Don't schedule major launches or in-person drops against conference weekends or July 24. Use Pioneer Day as a summer family-content window for casual and kids' product.

insights.title: Sunday is a soft retail day for many shoppers
insights.detail: A meaningful share of Utah households keep Sunday for family and church, and some local businesses close. Online sales and weekday or Saturday traffic carry more of the load than in most NBA markets.
insights.implication: Schedule in-store events, pop-ups and line-based releases for Friday or Saturday. Run Sunday through digital drops and e-commerce, not physical events.

insights.title: Cold-season layering is the core of the calendar
insights.detail: Salt Lake winters bring snow, inversion cold and a ski economy from roughly late November through April, at Park City, Deer Valley, Snowbird, Alta and Brighton. Summers are hot and dry. Outerwear, fleece and layers move well, and outdoor-brand fluency is a local status marker (Black Diamond is headquartered in Salt Lake).
insights.implication: Build Jazz product around quarter-zips, fleece, shells and beanies for October through March, with lighter tees and shorts for the short summer. Borrow outdoor trim and fabrics.

insights.title: A fan base that drives in
insights.detail: Jazz fandom reaches Ogden, Provo, Logan, St. George, southern Idaho, eastern Nevada and Wyoming. Many fans drive in from outside Salt Lake for games. The Delta Center is shared with the Utah Mammoth NHL team, which competes for the same fan dollar.
insights.implication: Concentrate game-night retail at the Delta Center team store. Stage satellite events in Ogden and Provo and at malls, and keep Jazz and Mammoth merchandising distinct.

insights.title: Win-now optimism is modest and star-led
insights.detail: Utah went 22-60 last season, and the market lines for 2026-27 sit near 35.5 wins. Fans follow individual players more than results. The Jaren Jackson Jr. trade and the arrivals of Darryn Peterson and Ace Bailey give the start of the season a fresh-face story.
insights.implication: Weight jersey and player-graphic product toward Markkanen, Jackson, Peterson and Bailey. Be ready to re-weight fast, depending on early-season performance.

insights.title: Value and secondhand are normal
insights.detail: Deseret Industries, Savers and local resale are widely used, and large families watch prices. Premium collectors exist, but mostly in a smaller sneaker-culture segment along the Salt Lake corridor.
insights.implication: Offer a clear good-better-best structure. Keep limited-edition collectibles, such as City Edition-specific pieces, in a separate tier for collectors.

extra.priceProfile: Utah's base is mostly middle-income, with high employment and low unemployment. Park City and the east-bench neighborhoods earn more, and the West Side earns less. Large households make fans value-conscious, so the right structure is a clear entry tier plus a small premium tier for collectors and visitors. State sales tax is 4.85 percent, with combined local rates in the Salt Lake area around 7.25 to 7.75 percent. Utah has no sales-tax-free weekend.
extra.jerseyBehavior: Families buy kids' and youth replica or swingman jerseys and tees before authentic jerseys, and Christmas is the biggest jersey window. Adult fans buy mostly tees, hoodies and caps. Authentic jerseys are a small collector segment, and knockoffs and secondhand pieces turn up. Expect new jersey demand for Peterson and Bailey as the rookie and second-year stories, with Markkanen and Jackson Jr. the safer adult choices.

factcheck.summary: Utah's dossiers held up on history, geography and league dates; every date matches CURRENT FACTS. The big miss, caught in a live check, was a navy-and-yellow Jazz identity. It is Mountain Purple, Midnight Black and Sky Blue, with highlighter yellow retired. Fanbase, uniform, retail-behavior and rhythm are fixed, and the strategy risk note is the editor's to change. Still open: small venues, named artists, Nike and athletic doors, the 2004-2022 uniform eras, and whether Utah plays the Nov 24-25 Cup nights.

issues.problem: The flagship community play rests on one partner, PIK2AR, a Pacific Islander health, education and advocacy nonprofit rather than a design or apparel body. The brief names no Latino partner at all. It folds Tongan, Samoan and Latino communities into one "West Side" designer pool and says they drive valley hoops, though the dossiers also describe their football culture and church-ward leagues. The sale points ("West Valley and Kearns athletic-chain doors") are unnamed.
issues.fix: Treat PIK2AR as a cultural-review and community-access partner, and recruit designers through a separate artist channel such as Salt Lake Arts Council rosters. Add a named Latino arts partner (verify Mestizo Institute of Culture and Arts or a similar group). Give Tongan and Samoan designers separate credit and approval rights. Soften the "hoop engine" claim to "a major part of West Side youth hoops and football". Name two real retail doors, or sell through the partners' own events, before committing.

issues.problem: A co-branded shell with Kuhl is not realistic, nor is framing Black Diamond and Kuhl as the status brands to cross-merchandise against. Nike would be partnering with an outdoor competitor on NBA-licensed product, and NBA marks run through league and team licensing. The idea also leans on Park City and Kimball Junction doors that serve visitors, not the statewide family fan the brief itself calls the core.
issues.fix: Drop the Kuhl co-brand and keep the idea inside Nike's own ACG and NBA outerwear lanes. Borrow the locals' technical-layer codes (shell cut, snap pockets, drawcords) without a partner logo. Put Park City at priority 3, and lead the line with the Delta Center store, Murray and Orem.

issues.problem: A salt-white base collides with the Association (white) uniform. On court, two nominally different jerseys would read as near-identical, and the NBA's color-contrast rules may limit it to certain games. North Arm Pink on a purple-trim Jazz jersey has no fan precedent in any dossier. Tying a jersey to a conservation partner (Great Salt Lake groups, state agencies) adds a politically live issue in Utah. The 2027-28 timeline is also tight, because City Edition design locks well before the preceding season ends.
issues.fix: Lead with the shale or deep-lake dark base, with salt white and pink as secondary colors. Or confirm with Nike's NBA uniform team that a white-base City Edition is permitted. Test pink with Jazz fans before committing, and keep it a small accent. Choose a nonpartisan conservation partner early, and treat the concept as a proposal that needs NBA and team sign-off.

issues.target: calendar[1] (Oct 30 Nuggets Cup Night) and opportunities[5]
issues.problem: The brief makes Fri Oct 30 the season-launch moment, then runs the first I-15 pop-up on Saturday Oct 31, which is Halloween. Halloween is a huge family and neighborhood night in Utah, so a family-focused pop-up competes with trick-or-treating. The brief also treats Oct 30 as the first home game without checking for an earlier regular-season home opener after the Oct 20 tip-off.
issues.fix: Anchor the launch to the actual first home game, and keep Oct 30 for the poster tee drop at Kilby Court only. Move the first corridor pop-up to Saturday Nov 7 or later. Add a kids' costume-friendly "Jazz Bear" angle only if the team wants it.

issues.problem: The brief plans Thanksgiving-week events around Cup nights, but each team plays only four group games across the five Fridays plus two extra nights. Nothing confirms that the Jazz are home on Nov 24, 25 or 27.
issues.fix: Build the Thanksgiving and Black Friday plan around retail and e-commerce, whatever the Jazz schedule says. Attach in-arena moments only to confirmed home dates once the schedule is read.

issues.problem: Saying "almost nobody connects" the colors to New Orleans overstates it. The "no jazz in Utah" joke is the most common local line, and the origin is routinely told. The throwback jersey and the Maravich credit also assume Nike can make Hardwood Classics-style product. Heritage jerseys sit with the team, the NBA and a separate heritage licensee, and Maravich's likeness needs his estate.
issues.fix: Reframe it as "the origin story is known but never designed": tell it on a label or insert, not a headline. Confirm which licensee holds Note and Mountain heritage jerseys before promising a classic jersey. Use the team mark, not the player name, for the New Orleans chapter.

issues.problem: The "alcohol-light" framing, dirty-soda cup and Fry Sauce Pink make Utah's religious culture the punchline. They also lean on third-party food and drink brands (Swig, Arctic Circle origins). The color story is thin too: pink and soda blue appear nowhere in Jazz identity or fan dossiers beyond the food notes. A local would read a joke about the state's dry reputation as an outsider's take.
issues.fix: Keep the all-ages venue story, which is strong (Kilby Court, SLUG, Gallery Stroll). Cut the soda, fry sauce and "drink-run" gags, or limit them to one wink on a sock. Take the poster palette from real SLUG and Kilby flyer ink colors, not food colors. Never present Latter-day Saint dietary practice as a joke.

issues.problem: The brief never mentions the Donovan Mitchell and Rudy Gobert years (the "Spida" look). That is the Jazz era most Gen Z fans and the many kids in their 20s grew up with. It sits between the Stockton-Malone and Peterson eras. It also ignores three local threads: the Salt Lake City Stars (G League) as an entry-price door, the Utah Starzz memory, and the Jimmer Fredette and BYU-Utah rivalry as feeders of local basketball identity.
issues.fix: Add a 2017-22 "Spida" era chapter to the heritage plan, as the bridge between Note-era nostalgia and Peterson. Use the Stars as a cheap in-person door. Treat Starzz as a women's heritage option via the WNBA (licensing needed). Keep college colors out of Jazz product, as the hoops dossier warns.

issues.target: opportunities[2] / calendar[10] (June Pride and Arts Festival)
issues.problem: A June Utah Pride Center artist piece sits on the calendar with no fan-base evidence and no budget. Nothing says how an NBA team would be received in the state's political climate. It reads as a festival checklist.
issues.fix: Either build it properly (a named LGBTQ+ Utah artist, paid, credited, partner-led and consistent with the team's own Pride programming) or remove it. Don't run it as a one-off tee.

issues.problem: A "Pioneer Day family weekend" tie-in sits beside July 24 with a "keep it secular" note. But the date is a state holiday rooted in Latter-day Saint pioneer history, and the brief already bans pioneer-trek imagery elsewhere. The summer plan is also the lowest priority yet takes two calendar rows.
issues.fix: Drop Pioneer Day from the product calendar and mention it only as a retail-traffic note. Keep Summer League to one tight beat.

issues.problem: The thesis treats the Delta Center as a stable home and omits ownership and arena context (Smith Entertainment Group, and the Utah Mammoth sharing the building). The brief lists Mammoth cues only in avoid lists, so a designer wouldn't learn that the arena store and crowd are shared with a second hometown team. Ownership and arena naming were not verified for this run.
issues.fix: Add one line on the shared arena and the hockey crossover. Verify the owner and arena name before any copy is written.

strengths: The family-multiples insight (young median age, big households, once-a-season trip, Deseret Industries thrift) is distinctly Utah and drives real product: youth and toddler depth, bundles, a small premium tier.

The calendar respects local rhythm. It has no Sunday or General Conference weekend events and launches on Saturdays. It also reads honestly that the Jazz are off the opening-night, Christmas and Specter stages, so 2026-27 is a local year.

The appropriation guardrails are strong and specific: no tatau or tapa, no temple or pioneer imagery, no Spiral Jetty without the Holt-Smithson Foundation, and paid, credited collaborators with approval rights.
The all-ages DIY lens (Kilby Court, SLUG Magazine, Gallery Stroll, Craft Lake City) gives the poster series real local credibility. The licensing language for the Note and Mountain marks is correct.
Treating the repeat gray gradient as a material story in outerwear, not a relaunch, is the right call for a repeat City Edition. It comes with usable hex palettes and pieces.
critique.summary: This brief is well grounded. Its family-first, cold-weather and local-rhythm reads would survive the swap test. The best ideas are the Peterson-Bailey family pack and the all-ages poster series. The weak points: the West Side partner mapping, an unrealistic Kuhl co-brand, a salt-white City Edition that clashes with the Association uniform, a Halloween clash for the first pop-up, and some Utah-as-punchline food humor. It also skips the Mitchell-Gobert era and the Salt Lake City Stars. Dates and partner claims all need live confirmation.
